apmo-2009-01.title: A monovariant: the sum of $1/t^2$
apmo-2009-01.body:
For the numbers on the board, let $S$ be the sum of $\frac1{t^2}$ over all numbers $t$ currently written.

When $r'$ is replaced by $a,b$ with $2r'^2=ab$:
$$\frac1{r'^2}=\frac2{ab}\le\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2},$$
because $\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}-\frac2{ab}=\left(\frac1a-\frac1b\right)^2\ge0$. So each operation does not decrease $S$.

At the start $S=\frac1{r^2}$. After $k^2-1$ operations there are $k^2$ numbers; let $s$ be the smallest. Every term of $S$ is at most $\frac1{s^2}$, so
$$\frac{k^2}{s^2}\ge S\ge\frac1{r^2},$$
which gives $s^2\le k^2r^2$, i.e. $s\le kr$. ∎

apmo-2009-02.title: A polynomial with known roots
apmo-2009-02.body:
Let $R(x)=\sum_{i=1}^5\frac{a_i}{x^2+i}$; we want $R(6)$. The hypothesis says $R(k)=\frac1{k^2}$ for $k=\pm1,\dots,\pm5$.

Let $P(x)=\prod_{i=1}^5(x^2+i)$ and $Q(x)=R(x)P(x)$, a polynomial of degree at most $8$. Then $P(x)-x^2Q(x)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $10$ that vanishes at the ten numbers $x=\pm1,\pm2,\dots,\pm5$ (there $x^2Q(x)=x^2R(x)P(x)=P(x)$). Hence
$$P(x)-x^2Q(x)=A\,(x^2-1)(x^2-4)(x^2-9)(x^2-16)(x^2-25)$$
for a constant $A$. At $x=0$: $P(0)=120$ and $(-1)(-4)(-9)(-16)(-25)=-14400$, so $A=-\frac{1}{120}$. Dividing by $P(x)$:
$$1-x^2R(x)=-\frac1{120}\cdot\frac{(x^2-1)(x^2-4)(x^2-9)(x^2-16)(x^2-25)}{(x^2+1)(x^2+2)(x^2+3)(x^2+4)(x^2+5)} .$$
At $x=6$:
$$1-36R(6)=-\frac{35\cdot32\cdot27\cdot20\cdot11}{120\cdot37\cdot38\cdot39\cdot40\cdot41}=-\frac{231}{374699},$$
because $\frac{35\cdot32\cdot27\cdot20\cdot11}{120\cdot40}=\frac{6652800}{4800}=1386$ and $37\cdot38\cdot39\cdot41=2248194$, and $\frac{1386}{2248194}=\frac{231}{374699}$ (divide by $6$; $374699=13\cdot19\cdot37\cdot41$).

Hence $36R(6)=1+\frac{231}{374699}=\frac{374930}{374699}$ and
$$R(6)=\frac{374930}{36\cdot374699}=\frac{187465}{6744582}.$$

**Answer:** $\dfrac{187465}{6744582}$.

apmo-2009-02.title: Solve the system (check)
apmo-2009-02.body:
Solving the $5\times5$ linear system directly (tedious but mechanical) gives
$$a_1=\frac{1105}{72},\quad a_2=-\frac{2673}{40},\quad a_3=\frac{1862}{15},\quad a_4=-\frac{1885}{18},\quad a_5=\frac{1323}{40},$$
and then $\frac{a_1}{37}+\frac{a_2}{38}+\frac{a_3}{39}+\frac{a_4}{40}+\frac{a_5}{41}=\frac{187465}{6744582}$, confirming the first method.

apmo-2009-03.title: The circle on diameter $PQ$ is orthogonal to all three circles
apmo-2009-03.body:
Let $O_i$ and $r_i$ be the centre and radius of $\Gamma_i$. Let $P$ be exceptional and let the lines $A_iB_i$ meet at $Q$.

**The feet $X_i$.** By symmetry in line $PO_i$, the chord $A_iB_i$ is perpendicular to $PO_i$; let $X_i$ be their intersection. Triangle $PA_iO_i$ has a right angle at $A_i$ and $A_iX_i$ is its altitude, so
$$O_iX_i\cdot O_iP=O_iA_i^2=r_i^2 .$$
In particular $O_iX_i<r_i<O_iP$: $X_i$ lies strictly between $O_i$ and $P$. So $P$ is not on line $A_iB_i$, and $Q\ne P$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $PQ$, centre $O$, radius $\rho$. Since $Q\in A_iB_i$ and $PX_i\perp A_iB_i$, we have $\angle PX_iQ=90^\circ$ (or $X_i=Q$), so $X_i\in\Gamma$.

**Power of $O_i$.** The line $O_iP$ meets $\Gamma$ at $X_i$ and $P$, both on the same side of $O_i$, so the power of $O_i$ with respect to $\Gamma$ is
$$OO_i^2-\rho^2=O_iX_i\cdot O_iP=r_i^2 .$$
Hence $\rho^2=OO_i^2-r_i^2$, which is the power of $O$ with respect to $\Gamma_i$, for $i=1,2,3$.

**$O$ is a fixed point.** So $O$ has equal power with respect to the three circles. The set of such points is the intersection of the radical axes. If the centres $O_1,O_2,O_3$ are not collinear, the radical axes meet in a single point, the radical centre $Z$; then $O=Z$ and $\rho^2=\text{pow}_{\Gamma_1}(Z)$, both independent of $P$. So every exceptional point $P$ lies on the one circle with centre $Z$ and radius $\sqrt{\text{pow}_{\Gamma_1}(Z)}$.

If the centres are collinear, the radical axes are all perpendicular to the line of centres; if they are distinct parallel lines there is no point with equal powers, hence no exceptional point. They cannot all coincide: put the centres at $(c_i,0)$ and the common radical axis at $x=0$; then $c_i^2-r_i^2=\kappa$ is the same for all $i$. If $\kappa\le0$ every disc contains the origin, so the discs overlap. If $\kappa>0$, then $|c_i|>r_i$ and two of the three centres, say $0<c_i<c_j$ (or the mirror image), are on the same side; then
$$c_j-r_j=\frac{\kappa}{c_j+r_j}\le\sqrt\kappa\le c_i+r_i$$
(because $c+\sqrt{c^2-\kappa}\ge\sqrt\kappa$ for $c\ge\sqrt\kappa$), so these two discs overlap — contradicting the hypothesis.

Hence all exceptional points, if any, lie on one circle (the circle centred at the radical centre and orthogonal to $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\Gamma_3$). ∎

apmo-2009-04.title: Fractions with denominator $k!$
apmo-2009-04.body:
For $k=1$ take $\frac21$. Let $k\ge2$ and $N=k!$. Consider
$$\frac{N^2+1}{N},\ \frac{N^2+2}{N},\ \dots,\ \frac{N^2+k}{N},$$
an arithmetic sequence with common difference $\frac1N$.

**Reduced forms.** For $1\le i\le k$ we have $i\mid N$, so $\gcd(N,N^2+i)=\gcd(N,i)=i$. Dividing numerator and denominator by $i$ gives the fraction in lowest terms:
$$a_i=\frac{N^2+i}{i}=\frac{N^2}{i}+1,\qquad b_i=\frac Ni,\qquad\gcd(a_i,b_i)=1 .$$

**Distinctness.** Both $a_i$ and $b_i$ are strictly decreasing in $i$, so the $a$'s are distinct and the $b$'s are distinct. Moreover for all $i,j$:
$$a_i\ge\frac{N^2}{k}+1=N\cdot(k-1)!+1>N\ge b_j .$$
So no $a_i$ equals any $b_j$, and all $2k$ numbers are distinct. ∎

apmo-2009-05.title: Look at blocks of $\ell r$ kilometres
apmo-2009-05.body:
Put Argovia at $0$ and Zillis at the point $d>0$ of the complex plane, so the car starts facing the direction $1$ (east). Turns happen only at integer distances, so the $(k+1)$-st kilometre ($k=0,1,2,\dots$) is driven in a constant direction $m_k\in\{1,i,-1,-i\}$, and a left turn multiplies the direction by $i$, a right turn by $-i$.

**Blocks.** Split the trip into blocks of $\ell r$ km. Turns occur at multiples of $\ell$ and of $r$, a pattern with period $\ell r$, and at the end of every block both robots turn simultaneously (no change). Inside a block, Larry turns at the $r-1$ multiples of $\ell$ in $(0,\ell r)$ and Rob at the $\ell-1$ multiples of $r$, and no two coincide ($\gcd(\ell,r)=1$). So all blocks are driven identically up to the starting direction, and each block rotates the car by $\ell-r$ quarter-turns to the right. Let $w=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell r-1}m_k$ be the displacement during the first block.

**Case $\ell-r\equiv2\pmod4$.** After one block the car has turned $180^\circ$, so the second block's displacement is $-w$; after two blocks the car is back at Argovia facing east, and the motion repeats. The path is closed of length $2\ell r$, so the car never gets farther than $\ell r$ from Argovia: it misses a Zillis farther away.

**Case $\ell-r\equiv\pm1\pmod4$.** The block displacements are $w,\ \mp iw,\ -w,\ \pm iw$, summing to $0$; after four blocks the car is back in its initial state. The path is closed of length $4\ell r$, so it stays within $2\ell r$ of Argovia: again Zillis may be missed.

**Case $\ell\equiv r\pmod4$.** Then $\ell,r$ are both odd (they are coprime), and $\ell\equiv r\equiv\varepsilon\in\{1,3\}\pmod4$, $\varepsilon^2\equiv1$. Before the $(k+1)$-st kilometre there have been $\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor$ left and $\lfloor k/r\rfloor$ right turns, so $m_k=i^{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(-i)^{\lfloor k/r\rfloor}$. Let $\alpha_k$, $\beta_k$ be the remainders of $k$ mod $\ell$ and mod $r$. From $\ell\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor=k-\alpha_k$ we get $\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor\equiv\varepsilon(k-\alpha_k)\pmod4$, and similarly $\lfloor k/r\rfloor\equiv\varepsilon(k-\beta_k)$. With $\omega=i^{-\varepsilon}$ (so $(-i)^{-\varepsilon}=\bar\omega$) and $i\cdot(-i)=1$:
$$m_k=i^{\varepsilon k}(-i)^{\varepsilon k}\,i^{-\varepsilon\alpha_k}(-i)^{-\varepsilon\beta_k}=\omega^{\alpha_k}\,\bar\omega^{\beta_k}.$$
By the Chinese remainder theorem, $k\mapsto(\alpha_k,\beta_k)$ is a bijection from $\{0,\dots,\ell r-1\}$ onto $\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}\times\{0,\dots,r-1\}$. Therefore
$$w=\Big(\sum_{\alpha=0}^{\ell-1}\omega^{\alpha}\Big)\Big(\sum_{\beta=0}^{r-1}\bar\omega^{\beta}\Big).$$
Four consecutive powers of the primitive fourth root $\omega$ sum to $0$, so the first sum equals $1$ if $\varepsilon=1$ and $1+\omega+\omega^2=\omega$ if $\varepsilon=3$; likewise the second is $1$ or $\bar\omega$. In both cases $w=1$ (as $\omega\bar\omega=1$).

So each block ends $1$ km further east, facing east again. The first kilometre of every block is driven facing east (no turn occurs before $\min(\ell,r)\ge1$ km into the block), so block number $j$ starts by driving along the segment from $j-1$ to $j$. Hence the car passes through every point of the ray towards Zillis and reaches it, whatever $d$ is.

**Answer:** exactly the coprime pairs with $\ell\equiv r\pmod4$, i.e. $\ell\equiv r\equiv1\pmod4$ or $\ell\equiv r\equiv3\pmod4$.
